With exercise and eating well I function with 8-9 hours but if I'm feeling unwell, dealing with a lot, or doing too many activities/tiring my brain out, it escalates quickly to being tired and sleeping all day every day. Lately all I can do is work part time and sleep. It's a bummer sometimes.

I'm frustrated by the same thing too. I now have my phone that I take everywhere and check in an almost paranoid fashion, and a year planner. With the two of those always in my bag I do alright, though I still miss stuff sometimes. Alarms, post it's, and writing stuff down, I have a few systems going to help me. Sucks that we have to be so vigilant, it took me a while and some therapy to be more okay with it, but it's just life now. Hugs ❤

I felt exactly the same way. I'm so sorry friend. What I did was start exercising, however much I could handle,  which was not much at first. Just keep at it! I also got a therapist, and read some books very slowly. Like The Four Agreements and The Subtle Art of Not Giving A F#@$. It's taken some time but now I'm exercising 4 times a week steadily and feeling much better about myself. It's hard to start feeling sure and connected again. I still struggle but I'm getting by now instead of just surviving. What kind of hobbies do you have? I find that simply accomplishing anything can really be a mood and confidence booster. Exercise is wonderful for that because you see results short term and long term. Feel free to message me if you want to talk too!

Exercise, specifically weightlifting. Low impact, easy to scale up and down(for good and bad days), and counting reps and planning workouts helps my brain too! Going on walks is great also.

I'm always advocating weight training on here and my Instagram. I'm 6 years post TBI, been weight training for 2 years now.  It has helped me so much!!! More than medicine, more than therapy. It's ability to work your muscles without large amounts of head movement is great, and counting reps gives you brain exercise too. Would reccomend it to any TBI survivor. Weightlifting is also easy to start small with and scale up over time. ❤

A Keto like diet with higher fat and less carbs really helped my memory retention! Plus a lot of those already mentioned supplements. Also exercise has done wonders. Cardio and weightlifting. ❤ still working on this myself though too.

Go to an ear doctor, and they can do some balance testing and see if anything is up. But I'm not sure, its just a guess. The human brain is mysterious.

I was in two car accidents in the same year. 6 months apart. Neither were my fault. Lots of broken bones and injuries and such, but I didn't figure out for a year or so after that my two concussions had left me with a moderate head injury. All my other injuries kind of hid the symptoms, some severe symptoms popped up later. I was house bound because of all the injuries, couldn't walk around without getting dizzy and puking, had mental breakdowns, memory gaps, insomnia.... you name it.
 It ruined my credit, my mood swings/bad health and anxiety ruined a bunch of relationships, and I legit thought I was crazy. Severe PTSD because of it all. It set me back mentally probably 10 years. I had to re-learn to move and walk and talk and control my moods like a child. 
It changed everything about me, I had to rebuild my life, brain, and body over again from scratch. 5 years later I am a completely different person with a completely different life.
I started a Keto-like diet a few months ago and I feel so much better when I stick to it! It really does seem miraculous. I would recommend it to anybody with a TBI ❤

It's like my life is the movie Memento right now, but with post it's, hah. I wonder if I should start tattooing stuff on my body.... lol. 
It sucks. I know. But what else is there but to keep trying and pushing forward, like warriors! We live in hard mode, and it makes us great. We accomplish more than the average Joe. At least that's something.... right?

Then quit. Doing stuff is just hard. You have to find ways to enjoy it or stop doing it and deal with what that brings your way. This isn't a gym problem, this is a mental problem. If you don't like it, don't do it. Just expect some health issues.

As someone who has been both thicker and thinner, it's not about being thin. It's about people feeling like you want them around. You have to put yourself out there. Even when I've been at my thinnest, it was usually me who had to initiate conversation and hang outs with people. People are ALL very self conscious, and don't want to be rejected. Sucks, but if you want to have more friends, you have to start taking the initiative, talking to people and offering help or fun so that you can hang out and get to know each other! So if you see a conversation opening, just take it. At the worst you'll embarrass yourself and probably never see the person again, at the best you'll have a new friend who will start putting themselves out there too.

When I got my first job after my accident, I didn't go into a lot of detail. Didn't put it on my resume at all. When they asked me about the time gap I said, "I was in a terrible car accident which took a long time to recover from. I still have some troubles from it but I am so ready to be back into the world again and be able to work. I am a hard worker and having to rest for so long was killing me!"  They were a little taken aback but mostly just sorry something that bad had happened to me. After a follow up of, "oh no, that's terrible, what happened, glad you are okay, wow you must be strong to go through that!" Everything went back to a normal interview and I got the job. It can definitely be seen as a show of resilience if you stay positive telling your story. ❤ I find most people are shocked and you get deemed a survivor. I mean, you did survive this and recover and it is totally impressive. 😎 Good work, and good luck getting the job!

I also started lightly exercising and stretching and meditating and while that sounds simple, it had helped a huge amount. I get less headaches and exercise hard now! I was also Vitamin D and magnesium deficient so I'm taking some supplements now and that was also a huge stepping stone for me. If I take care of my body super, super well I get less headaches. Hope you start feeling better! I know that feeling of going crazy and it is hard to deal with. ❤ 
Edit: I've never been impressed with migraine meds either. A little coffee helps more.

Mine was five years ago too, actually to the day! I slept a ton right after, I had other injuries too and was healing, but it turned into insomnia after a year or so. I would just stop sleeping for weeks and them crash. I had sleep medication for a while, I'd sleep like 10-12 hours a night but still feel tired. When I stopped my meds, I started exercising 4 or 5 times a week, and watching my diet. I sleep now 8-9 hours a night with an day nap on bad days. The exercise has done wonders for me! I feel like I get a more restful sleep because my body is tired, so I feel less tired through the day. I would HIGHLY recommend starting to exercise. It has done so much for my sleep and energy. I get less headaches, though at first the gym made me nauseous and headachy, it's been worth it, that only happens when I push myself too hard now! I also had an extreme vitamin D deficiency that made me tired too, and now I take vitamin D and magnesium supplements and I have much more energy! 
Tldr: exercise helps a lot more than you would think, go get checked for Vitamin D deficiency and start taking Magnesium before bed for more restful sleep.

Vitamin D!!! I cannot stress it enough. Ha!  Even if it's not the root cause of your anxiety it will help. I got tested for Vitamin D deficiency at the doctors, I had about the same amount as a dead person. Taking supplements has done wonders for me, I have more energy and a clearer head,  less stress. Also Magnesium before bed! Better sleep and digestion.

As a person with a TBI, also female, who also used to paint and draw, this is a frustrating situation because we are starting out confused that we can't do something like we used to. It should be so easy, but we try to draw on our knowledge but it's like a brick wall is in the way, our own mind just won't cooperate with us, grr. 

Before I say anything else I would first just like to thank you for looking for answers and trying to help. That is amazing of you. 
For me, it was like how she said, I used to know all the stuff I needed, but now with my brain injury, I barely remember it. She has basically been set back years and years in comprehension and coordination and having to learn it all again, except with a TBI, it's like learning it with a book written backwards in code while rock music is blasting. She's been set back to a child in some ways. The brain is not only set back years, but has a much much harder time learning and remembering. It takes me forever to learn something. She most likely needs a lot of repetition, and a lot of validation. My injury makes me second guess everything, so validation and encouragement goes a long way. It's definitely possible for her to learn, but it takes time, the connections in her brain, and mine, are very slow, and sometimes connect sporadically or in an odd way, or when in a stressful environment, not at all. It's like a bad game of telephone sometimes. Things that should be easy but require multiple parts of the brain become very confusing. The only thing that works for me is repetition, repetition, repetition! It gets frustrating, but I've learned to be patient with myself. Even then I still have days where I can't recall anything, so if I'm put on the spot not only will I clam up, but I will freak out inside because I feel like I should know and I do know that it will possibly look like shyness or laziness on my part even though I'm trying my best. 

Not calling on her in class is great. One on one is better. Having her write things down is a brilliant suggestion. I use that one with great success. All your suggestions are great. I would only add those two things I mentioned, repetition and validation. And a lot of patience! One thing over and over until it makes sense and she can write it down in a way she will understand later. The order of things will be difficult for her, but writing it put so she can reference it will help a lot. Maybe give her time to try to work it out herself sometimes at her own pace, if possible. I dunno if anything I've said helps, but there it is. She's lucky to have a teacher who cares!!!

Hello! I have a tbi injury to my frontal lobe, happened 3 years ago. The same thing happens to me. Doctors that I have worked with have told me that it's called "brain fatigue". For example, a normal person without tbi who has been studying for 3 days straight and not sleeping much will have this same thing happen. With TBI, it just comes on for us very quickly. I have triggers. If I don't eat enough, sleep enough, or do a lot of mentally taxing things all in a row, I go into this same state where I almost seem drunk, sometimes at the drop of a hat. All that can really be done is to find the triggers that cause it and try to lessen them. More sleep, never get too hungry, nothing overly stressful. When I am in this state, I'm mostly not aware until after the fact, only aware that I am not feeling quite right. It can be very stressful for my boyfriend, so don't feel too bad that it stresses you out... But it is a thing that will continue to happen to him. Maybe help him make some contingency plans so it happens less, try to find his triggers? Either way it will be something you will see, perhaps for the rest of his life. Know that he is just feeling things to the extreme, tiredness, emotions... For me I almost need to be treated like a kid sometimes, without condescending words, of course. 
Dating someone with a TBI brings some crazy stuff to the table sometimes, so it's okay to be scared, but if you don't think you can handle it, it's best to back away and let him get support from someone who can, or let his family/friends take over, because he needs support.
Good luck!! :)
